title: Hatch Chile Cumin Rub
finish: Red, earthy, cumin in the background
summary: New Mexico chile, cumin, oregano, salt. The desert rub for pork, goat, and a chuck roast that wants to be tacos.
story: Southwest barbecue does not always mean mesquite until the meat weeps. The seasoning is chile — Hatch if you can get it, New Mexico red if you cannot — with cumin and Mexican oregano. It loves pork shoulder, lamb, and beef cheek. Pair it with the red chile sauce, not a squeeze of KC.

items: ¼ cup New Mexico or Hatch chile powder (not generic chili powder)

steps.title: Toast the cumin
steps.body: Thirty seconds in a dry pan until fragrant, then grind. Pre-ground cumin from 2019 will taste like dust.

steps.title: Coat pork or beef
steps.body: A medium coat on a shoulder or chuck. Overnight if you can. The chile is the color; don't bury it in sugar.

proTips.text: Chili powder from the grocery aisle is cumin and oregano already mixed, often stale. Buy chile powder that is actually chile.

milestones.label: Mix
milestones.hint: Chile first, sugar last and light.

title: Chicago Rib-Tip Rub
summary: Paprika, celery seed, a little sugar. The South Side coat that sits under mild or hot sauce on rib tips and hot links.
story: Chicago barbecue is aquarium smokers, rib tips, hot links, and white bread. The rub is not the star — the sauce is — but the meat still needs salt, paprika, and the celery seed that says Midwest. Put it on tips and links, then sauce them like you mean it.

steps.title: Leave the celery seed whole
steps.body: It should pop. Ground celery seed disappears and tastes like a soup packet.

steps.title: On tips and links
steps.body: A medium coat. These cooks are hotter and faster than a packer. Then the mild or hot sauce, and more white bread than you think you need.

proTips.text: If you serve rib tips without sauce in Chicago you will be asked if you are lost.

title: Maryland Pit-Beef Rub
servings: About ½ cup — enough for a top round
summary: Salt, pepper, garlic, paprika. The Baltimore pit-beef coat — then you slice it rare and drown it in tiger sauce.
story: Pit beef is not brisket. It is top round over charcoal, charred outside, rare inside, shaved thin on a Kaiser roll. The rub is a steak rub with a little paprika. Sugar has no business here. The sandwich is the recipe; the tiger sauce is the other half.

steps.title: Coat the round
steps.body: A 3–4 lb top round, heavy coat, 1–4 hours in the fridge. Char over hot coals, then finish to 125°F for rare-mid. Rest. Shave thin against the grain.

proTips.text: If you smoke it to 200°F you have made dry roast beef. This is a grilled roast. Tiger sauce on the roll, onions if you have them.

title: Alder Brown-Sugar Rub
finish: Sandy, sweet-salty, made for fish and pork
summary: Brown sugar, salt, pepper, a little mustard. The Pacific Northwest coat for salmon, black cod, and a pork loin.
story: Up the coast the wood is alder and the meat is often fish. A little sugar helps a pellicle form and keeps salmon from tasting like a ham hock. This is a cure-adjacent rub, not a 14-hour bark builder. Pair with alder, not hickory.

steps.title: On salmon
steps.body: A light-medium coat. Fridge uncovered 45–90 minutes for a pellicle, then alder or apple at 225–250°F. Pull at 125–130°F.

steps.title: On pork loin
steps.body: A heavier coat, then 250°F to 140°F. Do not treat this like a shoulder rub.

proTips.text: Hickory plus this sugar rub on salmon is how you make candy ham that used to be a fish.

title: East Texas Sweet Sauce
finish: Thinner than KC, sweeter than Central Texas (which is to say: it exists)
summary: Ketchup, sugar, a little chili powder. The East Texas bottle they put on sliced beef — the one Central Texas pretends not to see.
story: West of the Trinity they will tell you sauce is a crutch. East of it, barbecue came with a sweet-hot tomato gravy and chopped beef sandwiches. This is thinner than Kansas City, a little chili-powder dusty, and meant to go on the meat, not just beside it. Use it on chopped beef, hot links, and the cousin who asked for sauce.

steps.title: Simmer 15–20 minutes
steps.body: Whisk, then low heat until it slightly thickens but still pours. East Texas sauce should soak chopped beef, not sit on top like frosting.

steps.title: On chopped beef
steps.body: Toss with hot chopped brisket or chuck. Extra in a squeeze bottle. Central Texas guests may sulk. Let them.

proTips.text: If a Hill Country pitmaster tastes this on brisket they will write an essay. Serve it anyway. Different state, same Texas.

milestones.label: On chopped beef
milestones.hint: Toss while the meat is hot.

title: Thin Chile Mop
finish: Thin, sharp, chile in the finish
summary: Vinegar, Worcestershire, chile. The mop Central Texas actually uses when they use anything — not a glaze, a basting liquor.
story: A mop is not a sauce you serve in a cup. It is a thin, hot liquid you slap on a hog or a shoulder to keep the surface alive. This one is chile and vinegar and Worcestershire, no ketchup. Beef can take a little. Poultry wants even less. Never mistake it for KC.

items: ½ cup beef stock or water
2 Tbsp chile powder or hot sauce
2 Tbsp melted beef tallow or butter

steps.title: Warm, don't reduce
steps.body: Heat until the salt dissolves and the fat melts in. If it thickens you have made a different sauce. Keep it rattly.

steps.title: Mop after bark sets
steps.body: Light passes every 45–60 minutes. Dirty mops from a raw-meat brush are how you get a science project. Keep a clean pot.

proTips.text: Opening the pit to mop costs you heat. If the bark is already perfect, leave the bottle on the table.

title: South Texas Pit Salsa
summary: Tomato, onion, jalapeño, lime. Not barbecue sauce — the bowl that belongs next to smoked brisket tacos.
story: South Texas does not always argue about molasses. Sliced brisket or barbacoa goes on a tortilla with a raw salsa that cuts the fat. Make it the day you slice. It will not keep like a cooked ketchup sauce, and it shouldn't.

items: 2 jalapeños, seeded and minced (leave seeds if you want it mean)

steps.title: Chop, don't puree
steps.body: You want pieces, not gazpacho. Salt, lime, rest 15 minutes, taste. More salt than you think — it is going on rich beef.

steps.title: Serve the same day
steps.body: Next to sliced brisket, tri-tip, or lamb. Warm tortillas. Not a glaze, not a mop.

proTips.text: If you cook this salsa you have made a different sauce. Raw is the point. The lime does the work ketchup does elsewhere.

milestones.label: 15-minute rest
milestones.hint: Salt blooms. Serve the same day.

title: Kentucky Black BBQ Sauce
finish: Almost black, thin, Worcestershire and lemon
summary: Worcestershire, lemon, vinegar, pepper. Western Kentucky’s black sauce — Owensboro dip by another name. No tomato. No molasses. Looks like engine oil.
story: In Owensboro they call it dip. Everywhere else in Kentucky they call it black barbecue sauce. Same bottle: Worcestershire, cider vinegar, lemon, black pepper, a little brown sugar. It is the sauce for smoked mutton and the honest one for a pork shoulder if sheep isn't on the block. Moonlite and Old Hickory built reputations on this color. If it tastes like ketchup you have left the state.

steps.title: Simmer, don't reduce to glaze
steps.body: Everything in a saucepan. Medium-low 12–15 minutes until the sugar dissolves, the butter melts in, and it goes a shade darker. It should still rattle in the pan. If it coats like KC molasses you went too far.

steps.title: Taste for lemon and pepper
steps.body: It should make your mouth water, not sit sweet. More lemon if it's flabby, more pepper if it's shy, a pinch of sugar only if the Worcestershire is harsh. Cool. Bottle. Fridge a month.

steps.title: Mop, dip, and table
steps.body: After bark sets, mop a mutton or pork shoulder every 45 minutes. When you chop the meat, toss it in a pan with a ladle of sauce — that's the dip. Put the rest in a bottle on the table. People from Kansas City will ask if you made a mistake. You did not.

proTips.text: Mutton is the original. A pork shoulder is the honest substitute. Brisket in black sauce is a conversation, not a tradition.
Worcestershire is the body. If you start with ketchup 'to darken it' you have made a different, worse sauce. Trust the bottle of Lea & Perrins.

milestones.label: Simmer
milestones.hint: Thin, dark, lemon bright. Butter just melted in.

milestones.label: Taste
milestones.hint: More lemon or pepper before you bottle.

milestones.label: Mop, then toss
milestones.hint: Chopped mutton or pork, hot, extra on the table.

title: Florida Sweet Sauce
finish: Orange-red, shiny, sweet with a citrus snap
summary: Ketchup, brown sugar, orange juice, honey. North Florida barbecue is sweet on purpose. The orange is what keeps it from tasting like Kansas City.
story: Florida pit sauce is tomato and sugar, then a squeeze of orange so it doesn't sit like candy. Honey, a little vinegar, Worcestershire. You glaze ribs and chicken with it, and you put a bottle on the table. This is not vinegar Carolina and it is not Texas. If someone from Austin winces, you are in the right state.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body:
Everything in a saucepan. Medium-low 15–20 minutes, stirring so the sugar doesn't scorch.
It should look orange-red and shiny, thick enough to coat a spoon, still pourable.

steps.title: Taste
steps.body:
Sweet first, then orange, then a little vinegar. More orange juice if it's heavy. More vinegar if it's candy.
Cool. Bottle. Fridge 2 weeks.

proTips.text: Fresh orange juice, not orange soda. Datil pepper instead of cayenne if you are in St. Augustine — sweet heat, same idea.

title: Mississippi Sweet Sauce
finish: Dark red, molasses-sweet, a little vinegar so it isn't dessert
summary: Ketchup, molasses, brown sugar. Delta wet sauce — sweeter than Memphis dry, darker than Florida orange.
story: Mississippi barbecue sits next to Memphis on the map and in the bottle: tomato, molasses, brown sugar, enough vinegar that it isn't frosting. You mop it on ribs and pulled pork. You put it on the table. This is the sweet the state actually cooks — not ranch-packet pot roast, not gator cayenne.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body:
Everything in a saucepan. Medium-low 15–20 minutes. Stir. Molasses will want to stick.
Dark red, shiny, thick enough to mop, not paste.

steps.title: Taste
steps.body:
Sweet and tomato first. Vinegar should show up on the second bite.
Cool. Bottle. Fridge 2 weeks.

proTips.text: This is a finishing sauce. Don't boil a shoulder in it for 8 hours. Smoke the meat, glaze late, extra on the table.

title: Ember Molasses Sauce
finish: Dark, sticky, sweet molasses first, onion and a little burn
summary: Your house bottle. Extra-sweet molasses, minced onion, a little heat. Tomato underneath.
story: This one is yours. Molasses leads hard — two-thirds of a cup — plus a quarter-cup of brown sugar so it reads sweet on ribs. Fresh minced onion cooked down in the pot. Vinegar and Worcestershire keep it from turning into frosting. Pair it with Ember House Rub: the rub builds the bark, this bottle goes on in the last twenty minutes.

items: ½ small yellow onion, minced fine
1 tsp hot sauce (more if you want it meaner)

steps.title: Sweat the onion
steps.body:
A splash of the vinegar and the minced onion in a saucepan on medium-low. 3–4 minutes until the onion looks wet and smells sweet, not raw.
Garlic in for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body:
Ketchup, molasses, the rest of the vinegar, brown sugar, Worcestershire, mustard, salt, paprika, pepper, cayenne, hot sauce.
Medium-low 15–20 minutes. Stir. Molasses sticks if you walk away.
It should look almost black-red and coat a spoon.

steps.title: Taste
steps.body:
Molasses and brown sugar first. Then onion. Then a little heat.
More brown sugar if you still want it sweeter. A splash of vinegar only if it sits heavy.
Cool. Bottle. Fridge 2 weeks.

proTips.text: Fresh minced onion is the difference between this and a powder-jar sauce. Don't swap onion powder back in unless the drawer is empty.
Brush it over Ember House Rub in the last 15–20 minutes. The rub is the bark. This bottle is the shine.

title: Ember Smoke Sauce
finish: Gold, glossy, sweet mustard with soft onion
summary: Honey mustard and onion — the Ember Smoke house bottle. Yellow mustard, honey, minced onion.
story: Ember Smoke Sauce is the honey-mustard house bottle: honey in the pot, onion cooked down until it sweetens, a little garlic. It still tastes like mustard, not cafeteria dip. Brush it on chicken and pork in the last fifteen minutes. Cold, it's a sandwich sauce.

items: ½ small yellow onion, minced fine

steps.title: Sweat the onion
steps.body:
Butter in a saucepan, medium-low. Minced onion 3–4 minutes until soft and sweet, not browned hard.
Garlic in for 30 seconds.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body:
Mustard, honey, vinegar, dark brown sugar, Worcestershire, salt, pepper, cayenne.
Medium-low 10–12 minutes, stirring, until it looks gold and glossy and the onion has melted into the sauce.

steps.title: Taste
steps.body:
Honey first, then mustard bite, then onion.
More honey if you want it sweeter. More vinegar if it sits heavy.
Cool. Bottle. Fridge 2 weeks.

proTips.text: Yellow mustard is the body. Dijon makes it sharper and more expensive-tasting. Either works. Don't use honey mustard from the bottle and call it this recipe.
Carolina Gold Mustard Sauce is already in this app — thinner, more vinegar, no honey. This bottle is the sweet cousin.

milestones.label: Onion soft
milestones.hint: Butter, minced onion, no hard brown.

milestones.label: Gold and glossy
milestones.hint: Honey and mustard married. Bottle it.

title: Ember House Rub
finish: Brick-red bark that takes Ember Molasses Sauce without turning to candy
summary: Your house rub, built to sit under Ember Molasses Sauce. Sweet paprika, dark brown sugar, mustard, and salt — the sauce does the rest.
story: The rub and the molasses bottle are a pair. The rub seasons and builds bark. The sauce goes on late. If both are candy, you hid the pork. So this mix keeps the dark brown sugar honest — equal sweet paprika, enough salt and dry mustard to cut the molasses when you glaze. Onion and garlic echo the minced onion in the sauce. Cayenne stays a rumor in both.

items: ¼ cup packed dark brown sugar

steps.title: Break up the sugar
steps.body:
Dark brown sugar clumps. Rub it through your fingers first so you don't get wet pockets in the jar.
Whisk everything until the color is even brick-red — no streaks of raw sugar.

steps.title: Jar
steps.body:
Airtight jar. Label it Ember House. Keeps 2–3 months.
If it turns into a brick, smash it and keep going. Sugar pulls moisture.

steps.title: On the meat
steps.body:
Thin mustard or oil as a binder.
A coat you can still see meat through.
Smoke for bark. In the last 15–20 minutes, brush Ember Molasses Sauce — thin coats, not a puddle.
The rub is the crust. The sauce is the shine.

proTips.text: Salt and paprika should equal the sugar, not lose to it. If you double the brown sugar you made competition candy, not this rub.
Made to wear Ember Molasses Sauce. Don't stack a second sweet rub and a second sweet sauce on the same rack.

milestones.label: Jared
milestones.hint: Label it so you don't grab the salt jar at 5 a.m.
